shared_rules: Educational only. Not legal advice. KeepMyProof and Spry Labs are not law firms.
Never promise an outcome, never say a record proves anything, never call anything court-ready or admissible.
Keep only what the reader already has or wrote; never snoop, record in secret or take what is not theirs.

chapters.title: Start here: keep what you already have
chapters.brief: Why a parent going through divorce or a custody case keeps dated copies and notes: memory fades under stress, and a lawyer, mediator or court self-help center can only work with what the parent can show them. The scope rule: keep copies of papers and messages you already have or that were sent to you, and notes you write yourself. Never go into a spouse's phone, email or accounts, never record anyone in secret, and never move or hide money; ask a lawyer what is allowed where you live. End with what the rest of the book gives them: a checklist, logs and the official court pages for their state.

chapters.title: How to keep a co-parenting log
chapters.brief: How to write log entries that stay useful: the same day, date and time first, what was planned and what actually happened, facts not feelings, the child's words in quotes only if the parent heard them directly, no guesses about the other parent's motives, short entries, corrections added as a new dated line instead of erasing. A good entry and a weak entry side by side, as an invented example with no names (use 'the other parent' and 'our child'). Keep the log in one place: a notebook, the printable log, or an app.

chapters.title: Saving messages, photos and screenshots from your own phone
chapters.brief: Practical steps for keeping copies of messages that were sent to the reader: screenshot the whole conversation with the date visible, keep the original messages on the phone too, export or email copies to themself where the app allows it, note in the messages log where each copy is saved, keep photos with their original dates, keep a backup in a second place. Never edit or crop a copy in a way that changes what it says. Only the reader's own phone and accounts.

chapters.title: Gathering the papers before you meet a lawyer or mediator
chapters.brief: Walk through the seven checklist groups in plain words (bank, retirement and debt statements; pay stubs and tax returns; household bills and expenses; home, car and property papers; agreements and court papers you already have; messages sent to you; the co-parenting log) and what a copy of each usually looks like. Suggest making one folder per group and one list of what is in it, and bringing copies, never the only original. Say plainly that what is needed varies by state and by case, and the lawyer or the court's self-help center says what matters for theirs.

chapters.title: Writing to the other parent when things are tense
chapters.brief: How to keep messages to the other parent short, polite and about the child and the schedule, because anything written may be read later by others. Answer the question asked, confirm times and places in writing, avoid sarcasm, threats and long arguments, wait before replying when angry, and use one channel when possible. No legal advice and no claims about what courts think.

chapters.title: Where to get help
chapters.brief: Point to the kinds of help that exist without promising any: the court's own self-help center or family law facilitator (most state court websites have one; the state pages at the back of this book link to official ones), legal aid organizations for people with lower incomes, the local bar association's lawyer referral service, and mediators. If anyone is in danger, call 911; protective orders are covered for each state at the back. Remind the reader that this book is not legal advice and that rules differ by state.
